whatItIs: A single Claude Code skill (`docs-reorg`) that takes one .md file path and classifies it against 4 Diataxis types plus a fifth "way-finding/landing" type the author added. SKILL.md drives a 4-step workflow: read the whole page (no skimming), score it into a 5-row table of low/medium/high confidence with a one-line reason per row, emit a plain-text SPLIT PLAN naming output pages and types for mixed pages, and — only for MkDocs — generate a two-file navigation shape (`.NAV.md` routing to typed folders, `index.md` as the real table of contents). Two reference files carry the substance: page-types.md holds the type table, a confidence rubric and per-type diagnostic signals with explicit "not a X if" counter-tests; reasoning.md restates the Diataxis compass and, more usefully, defines what mix actually means. The case study is one MkDocs section reorganized in two phases (rewrite in place, then move files), with eight task pages all classified how-to.
measures: Nothing. There is no accuracy number, no human-labelled ground truth, no inter-rater check, no eval harness, no tests. The only empirical artifact is case-study/docs-reorg-systemA.md, n=1 section, and its "Classification accuracy" section (lines 178-185) asserts the skill "correctly identified all eight task pages as how-to" with no ground truth other than the skill's own output. The case study closes (lines 277-282) by stating it was written by Claude from the diff of its own reorg — the subject grading itself. The 5-row confidence table is a self-report, not a measurement: it has no aggregation rule and no calibration.

practices.practice: Define a placement defect as a mode switch, not as a taxonomy violation: a page is broken when it forces the reader to be in two different modes at the same time. Test it with three concrete conditions — a practitioner following steps is interrupted by conceptual prose that asks them to stop and understand; a reader consulting a table falls into a walkthrough that asks them to follow along; a learner is handed an exhaustive table with no pedagogical purpose at that point. Explicitly do NOT count 'covers multiple topics' as a defect.
practices.locus: references/reasoning.md:110-121 (definition at 114, the three conditions at 116-119, the anti-false-positive at 112)
practices.evidenceForIt: Argued, not measured. It is a definition with a stated rationale ('the damage is not aesthetic — it is functional', line 121) and a deliberate carve-out against the obvious false positive. No data behind it.
practices.costAndCollision: Near zero: one sentence plus three bullets in the audit's failure taxonomy. It gives terse's `placement` failure class an operational test it currently has to infer. It does NOT import Diataxis: the test never names a type, so it survives the already-rejected 'Diataxis as a required pass'. Collides mildly with terse's 'be terse' if the three conditions are quoted in full — two would do.

practices.practice: Require two or more independent signals before a classifier may assign a label: one signal is noise, two is a pattern. Let confidence fall out of signal count rather than being an extra judgment the model makes.
practices.locus: references/page-types.md:24-36 (threshold stated at line 26; rubric table at 28-32)
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. No calibration data, and — see weaknesses — the rubric this threshold feeds contradicts itself across three files, so take the threshold, not the rubric.
practices.costAndCollision: One line. Applies directly to terse's audit classifying each wrong answer as lie / placement / findability: the rule stops a single weak cue from deciding the class. Cost is a small increase in unclassified items, which is the right trade.

practices.practice: Ship every diagnostic signal with its known false positives attached. Concretely for prose: declarative sentences OUTSIDE steps are a mix signal, declarative step results INSIDE steps are not; and informal future tense ('you will see a confirmation') is not a learning-outcome signal — only a deliberate upfront statement of what the reader will have achieved by the end of the page counts.
practices.locus: references/page-types.md:40-59 (mood table 44-47; the two carve-outs at 49-51 and 57-59); per-type counter-tests at 70, 79, 88, 97, 105
practices.evidenceForIt: Argued from authoring experience ('many pages written by non-tech writers use future tense…', line 57). Not measured. The counter-test pattern — every type definition ends with an explicit 'Not a X if: …' line that names the type it is most confused with — is the transferable part.
practices.costAndCollision: Cheap and mechanical. The general form ('each rule states what it is NOT evidence of') is worth adopting across terse's audit signals; the specific verb-mood content is docs-flavoured and only pays off if terse ever classifies page purpose. Collides with terse's brevity: each rule roughly doubles in length when its carve-out is attached. Worth it — an unqualified signal produces confident wrong labels.

practices.practice: Forbid the repair pass from inventing content: a split or repair plan only redistributes text that already exists on the page. If a gap is found, name the gap; do not fill it.
practices.locus: .skills/docs-reorg/SKILL.md:167 ('Do not invent content — the split plan only redistributes what exists on the page'); reinforced by SKILL.md:77-78 keeping the plan to titles and types
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted as a hard rule, with no supporting data — but it is a guardrail, and the failure it prevents (a model inventing plausible API facts while 'improving' a doc) is the exact way terse's repair pass could turn a findability failure into a lie.
practices.costAndCollision: One line in revise's pass 4. Directly protects terse's own measurement: the audit derives its answer key from CODE, so any invented sentence in repair is an unmeasured lie the next audit will catch as a regression. No collision.

practices.practice: Give the classifier a licensed escape hatch: when no label reaches threshold, output 'unclassifiable' and name the boundary that is unclear rather than forcing the nearest label.
practices.locus: .skills/docs-reorg/SKILL.md:54-57 ('If confidence is low across all types, flag the page as unclassifiable. Do not force a classification.')
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. Note the repo does not obey its own rule cleanly — see weaknesses — but the instruction itself is sound and is the kind of permission a model needs stated explicitly or it will always pick something.
practices.costAndCollision: Two lines. Relevant to terse's failure classifier, where a forced lie/placement/findability label on an ambiguous miss pollutes the count the whole method rests on. Slight collision with terse's bias to a decisive answer.

practices.practice: Sequence a restructuring so the path-changing step comes last: first rewrite and add files in place (no path changes, so no links break), validate the build, and only then move files, updating every cross-reference.

weaknesses:
Do not lift the classifier whole; four things are wrong with it.

1. The confidence rubric contradicts itself across three files, so the output's meaning is undefined. page-types.md:32 says Low confidence = "signals are spread across two or more types with no clear dominant — this is the mixed content flag". SKILL.md:54 says low confidence across all types means the page is **unclassifiable**. case-study:191-192 and 223-224 say a mixed page registers "high on wayfinding, medium on how-to, medium on explanation" and that "a mixed page registers medium-or-high confidence on multiple types, which is itself the diagnosis". Three incompatible readings of what a low/medium row means for the one case the skill exists to catch. A rubric whose own author's three files disagree has not been run against anything that would have exposed the disagreement — which matches the absence of any eval.

2. Zero measurement, and the one case study is the subject grading itself (case-study:277-282: written by Claude from the diff of its own reorg). The "Classification accuracy" claim (178-185) has no ground truth. Against terse's own bar — six reader questions, 3 right to 6 right — this repo offers nothing comparable.

3. The primary output is an audit artifact, not a rewrite. Step 2 produces a 5-row table of labels and Step 3 produces a list of page titles; SKILL.md:77-78 explicitly says "Keep it lean — titles and types only" and 167 forbids touching the prose. It names what a page *is* and never says what sentence to change. That is precisely the failure mode already measured — published standards producing audits rather than rewriting — so this is confirming evidence for the existing rejection, not a counterexample to it.

4. Scope drift and self-inconsistency signal low rigor. SKILL.md Step 4 (lines 80-157) is MkDocs `.NAV.md` plumbing irrelevant outside that toolchain, and it is the longest step in the file — half the skill is navigation YAML-adjacent boilerplate rather than classification. The skill's own README tells the user to install it under `.skills/content-classifier` (README.md:16) when the directory is `docs-reorg`, and the root README links `case-study/report.md` (README.md:38) which returns HTTP 404 — verified. A docs-quality skill whose own docs fail a link check and a path check has not been audited by its own standard.

Bottom line: the taxonomy and the scoring table are not worth taking; the mix-as-mode-switch definition, the two-signal threshold, the signals-ship-with-their-false-positives discipline, and the do-not-invent-content guardrail are, and none of the four requires adopting Diataxis.
